job.title: Analyst II, Supply Chain - Corporate - US (Open)

realStack: Microsoft Excel (intermediate) — the only hard tool requirement; spreadsheet/financial modeling, cost build-ups, scenario comparison
Microsoft Access (preferred) — relational storage/querying of larger supply-chain datasets that outgrow Excel
Microsoft PowerPoint (preferred) — packaging scenario results, cost-savings cases, and recommendations to internal/external stakeholders
Mixed-integer-programming network-optimization tools: Llamasoft Supply Chain Guru, Supply Chain Strategist, or equivalents (strongly preferred) — the actual modeling engine for the role
Quantitative/statistical techniques: regression analysis, spreadsheet modeling, statistics (theoretical knowledge preferred)
Supply-chain domain frameworks: category management, redistribution analytics, steady-state optimization, transportation-network design
Internal cost/operational data feeds and stakeholder-supplied datasets (current-state costs, lanes, volumes) that must be sourced and validated
Project/portfolio coordination across a matrixed, cross-functional organization (multiple concurrent modeling projects)
coreResponsibilities: Act as business/subject-matter expert for supply-chain design, modeling, and analysis
Source and validate the data needed for analysis from internal and external stakeholders
Build, run, and compare supply-chain scenarios in optimization tools (category management, redistribution, steady-state, transportation networks, ad-hoc)
Recommend the most profitable and executable future-state scenario and quantify projected cost-savings impact
Manage multiple modeling projects concurrently in a fast-paced, shifting-priority environment
Engage customers to understand their business model and capture current-state costs and assumptions
Develop strategies, assumptions, and analysis deliverables with key stakeholders
Hand off from analysis to execution with operations teams, and persuade internal/external customers to adopt the recommended change
statedVsRealGaps: Hard-requirement floor vs. real scope: only 'intermediate Excel' is required, while the actual work is MIP-based network optimization (Llamasoft/Guru) — the genuinely role-defining skill is merely 'strongly preferred,' so the stated bar undersells the job.

Title vs. mandate: framed as a medior 'Analyst II,' but the responsibilities (own multiple projects, be the SME, build the business case, and 'sell' change to internal/external customers) read more like an analyst-consultant hybrid leaning senior.

JD is partly redacted/templated: minimum years of experience, zip, and travel % are blank, and all company-scale figures are stripped ('over [ ] associates', 'fleet of over [ ] vehicles') — the experience/seniority bar can't be read precisely from the text.

Quant rigor is soft-gated: statistics/regression knowledge is only 'preferred,' yet 'strong quantitative problem solver who can interpret large data sets' is listed as an intrinsic capability — the must-have analytical depth is asserted in soft language rather than required qualifications.

'External customers' is ambiguous: likely Sysco's foodservice customers receiving supply-chain consulting, which adds a commercial/relationship dimension not reflected in the otherwise analytical qualifications.
riskAreas: Mis-hire risk from the requirement/scope mismatch: an 'intermediate Excel' floor can attract spreadsheet analysts who can't operate MIP network-optimization tools, while the title may deter the experienced optimization modelers the role actually needs.

Tooling dependency: the core engine (Llamasoft Supply Chain Guru / Supply Chain Strategist) is only 'preferred,' so expect ramp-up time and reliance on tool licenses/availability; few candidates arrive fluent in it.

Rare combined profile: deep quantitative/optimization skill PLUS stakeholder management and 'selling' change is an uncommon blend — risk of finding strong pure-analysts or strong pure-consultants but not both.

Execution/data risk outside the analyst's control: deliverables hinge on obtaining and validating data from internal and external parties, and on operations actually adopting the recommended future state.

Ambiguous seniority bar: blank years-of-experience and a redacted JD make leveling and comp calibration error-prone; 'relevant Sysco experience in lieu of a degree' widens the funnel but loosens the screen.
Fast-paced, matrixed, multi-project load raises burnout/throughput risk if staffed at a true medior level without senior support.
analysis.reflection: This is a genuine supply-chain network-design role at a global foodservice distributor, and in its own terms the work is high-complexity: mixed-integer-programming optimization of redistribution and transportation networks, multi-scenario cost modeling, and quantified cost-savings cases delivered into a matrixed organization. The real toolset is not just Office — it centers on optimization platforms (Llamasoft Supply Chain Guru / Supply Chain Strategist) backed by Excel, Access, statistics, and PowerPoint for the business case. The clearest tension between what's stated and what the role really demands is the gap between a very low hard-requirement floor (intermediate Excel; everything quant or optimization-specific is only 'preferred') and an aspirational mandate that asks the person to be the SME, run multiple projects, project savings, and persuade customers to change. Combined with a partly redacted JD (blank experience/zip/travel, stripped scale figures), this makes leveling and screening the main hiring risks: the posting could plausibly be filled by an under-qualified spreadsheet analyst or demand a near-consultant — the requirements section doesn't disambiguate. A sound hire screens for actual optimization-modeling experience and the analyst-plus-influence blend, regardless of the soft language in the JD.

case.title: Relieve the Front Royal RDC: redistribution & landed-cost scenario analysis
case.brief: You are the Analyst II on a redistribution study for a foodservice distribution network. Supply-chain operations has flagged that the Front Royal redistribution center (RDC) is running over its throughput ceiling, and leadership wants a recommended future-state with a cost-savings case they can take to the operating teams. You've been handed a partly-cleaned workbook from the ops stakeholder plus a master-data export from the team's Access database. The materials are real-world messy: the stakeholder's numbers don't fully tie to the master data, and the cost model carries some inherited assumptions. The provided materials fit this role directly — you act on them the way the role does: validate the data, set up a defensible current-state baseline, model and compare future-state scenarios, pick one, size the savings, and sell it. The 1.5h cap is real, so scenarios can be directional/back-of-envelope with assumptions stated explicitly — depth is expected in your judgment (what you trust, what you optimize for, what's actually executable), not in modeling volume. You do NOT need Supply Chain Guru / a MIP solver to finish; Excel is sufficient for the timebox — but note where you would escalate to the network-optimization tool and why a spreadsheet stops being enough. The numbers you should not have to be told: read the materials before you model.
case.repoSeed:
A small starter pack handed over for the study:
- Current_State_Network.xlsx — tabs: 'Lanes' (origin DC → customer zone, miles, mode, current outbound freight rate), 'Volumes' (monthly cases and weight by customer zone), 'Cost_Buildup' (per-case inbound, warehousing, outbound freight, handling rolled to a total landed cost), 'Assumptions' (fuel surcharge factor, days-of-supply target, warehouse labor rate), and a near-identical leftover tab 'Cost_Buildup_2019_archive'.
- DC_Master.csv — exported from the team's Access DB: DC list with weekly throughput capacity (cases/week), fixed facility cost, and variable handling cost per case for Front Royal and two candidate alternate DCs.
- data_dictionary.md — one page defining each field and its unit (note: outbound freight is quoted per hundredweight/cwt; volumes appear in both cases and weight).
- stakeholder_handover.txt — short note from supply-chain ops: 'Front Royal is at ~112% of throughput, has been for two quarters. Need a future-state and a savings number for the Q3 review. Volume file is what we pulled last month — should be close.'
Known rough edges left in on purpose: one customer zone is assigned to two DCs in the Volumes tab; a couple of Lanes rows have the freight rate entered per case rather than per cwt; the stakeholder Volumes total doesn't reconcile to DC_Master throughput.
tasks: Validate before you model. Reconcile the 'Volumes' tab against DC_Master.csv throughput and against the 'Cost_Buildup' totals. Identify every discrepancy you can find — at minimum the customer-zone-to-DC double assignment and any unit inconsistencies in the Lanes outbound freight rates — decide for each which source you trust and why, and list the specific data you would request from the ops stakeholder before locking a baseline.

Establish a defensible current-state landed-cost baseline (inbound + warehousing + outbound freight + handling), both per case and in total, using the corrected data. State the objective function you are optimizing for explicitly, and call out which Cost_Buildup inputs and assumptions you relied on.

Model and compare two future-state scenarios that relieve the Front Royal over-capacity — for example, redistributing a share of volume to an alternate DC vs. rebalancing outbound lanes/mode — on landed cost, service (days/miles), and executability. Recommend one, project the annualized cost-savings vs. baseline, and write a one-page stakeholder-facing summary that would persuade operations to adopt it. Note where this analysis would warrant escalation to a network-optimization tool (Supply Chain Guru / Supply Chain Strategist) rather than Excel.

Keep a short DECISIONS log alongside your work: for every open call — the objective function, which data source you trusted on each conflict, what you treated as in/out of scope (e.g. whether opening or closing a DC was allowed), and any assumptions you fixed to move forward — record what you chose, the alternative you rejected, and the one question you would have asked the team.

coverProbes.where: The handover asks for 'a future-state and a savings number' but never states what to optimize for, and never bounds scope (is opening/closing a DC on the table, or only re-routing existing volume?).
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate names the objective function up front (lowest landed cost vs. service-days vs. fastest-to-execute), pins the scope boundary, and flags that 'most savings' and 'most executable' can point to different scenarios. A naive response silently optimizes for the single biggest cost number and reports it as the answer without acknowledging the trade-off or that it made a scope assumption.
decisionSpace: Optimize for lowest total landed cost — maximizes the headline savings but may push volume to a DC ops can't realistically absorb this year.
Optimize for executability/service within an acceptable cost band — smaller savings but adoptable now, fitting the 'sell to operations' mandate.
Present a frontier of 2 scenarios (cost-max vs. execute-now) and let leadership choose — most honest, costs time against the 1.5h cap.

coverProbes.where: The stakeholder 'Volumes' tab doesn't reconcile to DC_Master.csv throughput, and one customer zone is assigned to two DCs — so the same demand can be counted twice or attributed to the wrong facility.
coverProbes.reveals: A good candidate detects the conflict, makes an explicit, reasoned choice of which source governs (and for which fields), and de-duplicates the double-assigned zone before baselining. A naive one-shot model ingests the Volumes tab as-is, inheriting the double count and an inflated baseline that makes any scenario look like savings.
decisionSpace: Trust DC_Master as the system of record for capacity/assignment and treat the Volumes tab as directional — clean, but may discard recent real demand shifts ops knows about.
Trust the stakeholder Volumes tab as the freshest demand pull and reconcile capacity to it — current, but propagates the double-assignment unless caught.
Use master data for structure/assignment and the Volumes tab for magnitudes, reconciling the delta and flagging it for the stakeholder — most defensible, more work.

coverProbes.where: 'Cost_Buildup_2019_archive' is nearly identical to the live 'Cost_Buildup' tab and easy to grab by mistake, and the 'Assumptions' tab carries a hardcoded fuel-surcharge factor that reads as stale.
coverProbes.reveals: A candidate who reads the materials notices the archive tab and the dated surcharge, sources current values (or explicitly flags them as assumptions to confirm), and documents it. A naive generator links formulas to whichever tab it grabbed first and carries the stale surcharge straight into every scenario, so the error scales with volume.
decisionSpace: Use the live Cost_Buildup and refresh the fuel surcharge to a current figure — most accurate but requires sourcing/justifying the new value.

Keep the existing surcharge but flag it as an assumption-to-confirm and hold it constant across baseline and scenarios so the comparison stays apples-to-apples — fast and internally consistent, absolute savings may be off.
Run a sensitivity on the surcharge to show whether the recommendation flips — most rigorous, costs time against the cap.

coverProbes.where: Outbound freight is per cwt but a few Lanes rows are entered per case, and the lowest-cost reallocation can exceed the alternate DC's weekly throughput in DC_Master.csv. A clean-looking model totals correctly yet is wrong on units and proposes an un-executable move.
coverProbes.reveals: A careful candidate cross-checks freight cost against both weight and cases to catch the per-cwt/per-case mismatch, and tests the recommended reallocation against the receiving DC's capacity before claiming the savings. A naive submission passes a shallow 'does it sum?' check, reports an over-stated saving, and recommends a future-state the network physically can't run.
decisionSpace: Normalize every lane to per-cwt using weight and re-derive freight — most correct, requires reconciling the cases-vs-weight columns.
Cap any reallocation at the receiving DC's stated throughput and re-optimize within capacity — protects executability, leaves some theoretical savings on the table.
Surface both the unit fix and the capacity constraint as caveats and present a capacity-feasible recommendation with the unconstrained number shown for context — most transparent, more analysis time.
